newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: OAU to discuss Sierra Leone and Zaire.
newsitem.headline: OAU to discuss Sierra Leone and Zaire.

text.p: African leaders, growing more outspoken at problems in their own back yard, condemned Sierra Leone's latest coup as their annual get-together opened on Monday.

They also applauded Congo leader Laurent Kabila -- basking in his new-found status at the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) summit -- and cautiously welcomed his military takeover last month of what was Zaire.
As fighting raged in Freetown between Sierra Leonean coup forces and Nigerian troops sent in to oust them, U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan said the military takeover a week ago had revolted him.
"Africa can no longer tolerate and accept as faits accomplis coups against elected governments and the illegal seizure of power by military cliques," he told heads of state at the Zimbabwe summit.
"Armies exist to protect national sovereignty and not to train their guns on their own people," he said.

The 47 states represented in Harare delayed discussion of the successful takeover in Congo and the collapsing coup in Sierra Leone until Tuesday and some delegates said privately delegates were battling to find common ground on the issues.
One U.N. source said efforts to resolve the confrontation in Sierra Leone would be dealt with by the Economic Community of West African States (Ecowas), whose members would brief the OAU on Tuesday.
South African President Nelson Mandela appealed to the coup leaders to guard civilian lives. In remarks to Reuters he said, "It would be a tragedy if civilians were caught in the crossfire."
But he said he had no intention of intervening unless he was specifically asked to do so.
Nigeria, Ghana and Guinea sent troops to Sierra Leone to try to persuade or force Major Johnny Paul Koromah to restore power to elected President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.
"Where democracy has been usurped, let us do whatever is in our power to restore it to its rightful owners, the people," Annan said in an apparent endorsement of the intervention.

OAU Secretary General Salim Ahmed Salim, who was later elected for an unprecedented third four-year term, said Africa had at last reached a point where the majority of its governments were democratic and economic growth could follow.
"The recent coup d'etat in Sierra Leone...is an unacceptable attempt to defy this trend. Everything must be done to restore constitutional legality in that country," he said.
Nigeria leader General Sani Abacha, who himself took power by force, was expected at the OAU's 33rd summit in Zimbabwe's capital Harare but did not arrive for Monday's opening session.
An OAU official said Abacha and Ghana's Jerry Rawlings had stayed home to handle the crisis in Sierra Leone.
Kabila, who ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko from the vast country he had run as a fiefdom for 32 years, was welcomed with applause and hugs when he arrived.
African leaders welcomed the Congo's change of power, one of the most significant in Africa's post-colonial history, but stopped short of a clear vote of confidence in Kabila.
Annan told Kabila, who wore an open-necked blue safari suit, that he was pleased with his "commitment to constitutional rule and to the holding of democratic elections".

But the Ghanaian U.N. chief added: "It is necessary even now that the protection of human life and full respect for human rights are given the highest priority, and that the rule of law should quickly return to that vast and vibrant country.
"The United Nations asks that we may tend to the weak and the displaced so that this new beginning may be an affirmation of the sanctity of life."

Mandela, who went to Harare mainly to discuss ways for South Africa to bolster the new Democratic Republic of Congo, left without more than a passing chat with Kabila after the Congo president kept him waiting for over an hour.
OAU spokesman Ibrahim Dagash said the summit would discuss Africa's security problems in closed session on Tuesday and would base any decisions on Sierra Leone on the Ecowas report.
